pg008_narration1: Preface This textbook, Book-keeping for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form Two students in the United Republic of Tanzania. It is written in accordance with the 2023 Book-keeping Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education Form I-IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MoEST). It is a revised edition of Book-keeping for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form Two that was published in 2023 in accordance with the 2016 Book-keeping Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education Form I-IV, issued by the MoEST. The book consists of four chapters, namely: Recording cash and banking transactions, Correction of Book-keeping errors and the Trial balance, Reconciling bank account with cash book balances and Budgeting and budgetary control. Each chapter contains text, worked examples, activities, exercises and revision exercises. You are encouraged to do all the activities, exercises, revision exercises as well as other assignments provided by your teacher. Doing so will enable you to develop the intended competencies. Additional learning resources are available in the TIE e-Library at https://ol.tie.go.tz or ol.tie.go.tz Tanzania Institute of Education
pg009_narration1: Chapter One Recording cash and banking transactions Introduction Keeping records of cash and banking transactions is essential for everyone. To manage your pocket money properly, you must keep some records of your transactions. Businesses have systems to record receipts and payments of cash and banking transactions that form part of their day-to-day operations. In this chapter, you will learn the meaning of cash and banking transactions, the types of cash book, and preparation of cash books (single-column, two-column, three-column, and the petty cash books). The competencies developed will enable you to record cash and banking transactions in different types of cash books appropriately. Think Operating a business without recording cash and banking transactions Meaning of cash and banking transactions Cash transactions is a form of payment/ receipt in which cash money is exchanged for goods or services during the time of purchase, sale or any other payments/ receipts. This transaction uses physical money such as banknotes and coins. Examples of cash payments are; Juma buys motor vehicles and machinery for his business and then immediately pays the seller a total amount TZS 14,000,000, in cash, Juliet pays cash TZS 300,000 for light and heating charges to Jm Co. Ltd. Another example on cash receipt, a company borrows money from the bank and received it in cash. Cash transactions involve the inflow of money (cash receipts) and outflow of money (cash payments). Cash receipts refer to money received, for example, the sources of cash receipts for a business may include cash sales, customer payments, or refunds. On the other hand, cash payments represent money spent including expenses, supplier payments, and debt settlements. Cash transactions offer a dependable and accessible payment method, especially for individuals who do not have access to digital payments. They are also useful in
pg010_narration1: situations where technology fails, such as internet problems or power failure. This ensures that payments can still be made without disruption. Banking transactions refer to financial transactions that involve the flow of money into or out of a customer’s, or business’s bank account. This includes money deposits, transfers, withdrawal payments, and other financial transactions carried out in a bank account. For example, a customer deposits TZS 400,000 from weekly sales into the bank for personal savings, a company transfers TZS 800,000 using SimBanking for services received, and a business venture withdrawals TZS 9,000,000 from the bank for paying operating expenses. Mobile money transactions are treated as banking transactions because they have similar features. Banking transactions provide a safe and secure way to handle money. They reduce the risk of loss or theft associated with holding cash. They also offer accurate record-keeping of transactions, which helps individuals and businesses to track their revenues and expenses effectively. Activity 1.1 Visit any business operating in your locality and observe how the business activities are conducted. Based on your observation, identify different cash and banking transactions occurring in the business. Cash book and its purpose Cash book is a book used for recording the flow of cash into and out of the business. A cash book includes all accounts that record receipts and payments of cash for a business. Book-keeping practice recognises cash book as a book of original entry and as a ledger. It is therefore important to note that reference to cash book in this textbook is applicable to both, the case where the intended record is a journal and the case where it is a ledger. The purpose of the cash book is to ensure that up-to-date records of cash status are available at any point in time. When the cash status is readily available, it assists the management of the business to: (a) properly plan for different transactions. (b) know the financial position (liquidity) of the business. (c) decide on whether they can make business expansion. (d) decide on whether they need a loan from external sources. Types and preparation of cash books
pg010_narration2: The traditional version of cash book is the cash account. Development in modern payment systems and controls has brought about a necessity to have different types of cash books, which are: (a) Single-column cash book (b) Two-column cash book (c) Three-column cash book (d) Petty cash book

Single-column cash book Single-column cash book comprises of cash account and bank account when they are prepared separately. Cash account You may recall that you probably used some cash for commuter bus fare to school in the morning. You also probably spent some cash to buy some tea or snacks during tea break, and you hopefully enjoyed that! Did not you? What you did was paying cash to the tea vendor or service provider in return for goods or services. On the other hand, the tea vendor received cash from you and gave you a cup of tea. Many small businesses have a significant part of Example 1.1 their transactions conducted on cash basis. When buying goods for sale, paying for rent, electricity, water and other utilities for their businesses, these traders make a number of cash payments. They also collect cash from different transactions involving selling of goods or services. Records for such cash receipts and payments are kept in a cash account. The cash account, like any other ledger account has a debit side and a credit side. Being an asset account, the double entry rule for recording transactions in the cash account is: (a) Debit cash account for receipts of cash (increase in asset). (b) Credit cash account for payment of cash (decrease in asset). Example 1.1 shows how transactions are recorded in a cash account. Support your explanation with a simple illustration showing its format. Bank account Business transactions can be done through bank systems. Businesses have a choice to open different types of bank accounts. The most convenient and popular type of bank account that a business would prefer is a current account. A current account is an account in which withdrawal of cash is made using a cheque. A cheque is an instruction issued to a bank to pay a specified amount of money to a specific person or a bearer. A cheque has three main parties involved. The parties are the drawer, the payee and the drawee. These are described as follows: Drawer – is the person (bank account holder) who writes or issues a cheque. By issuing or drawing the cheque, the drawer instructs the bank to pay money from the bank account. Drawee – is the drawer’s bank that receives instruction to pay the amount stated on the cheque. The bank issues a cheque book to the current account holder. Each time the current account holder wants to issue a cheque, he/she uses one leaf from the cheque book and fills in the particulars of the payment. Payee – this is the person who is paid the amount written on the cheque. A cheque instructs the bank to pay this person. A cheque would normally mention the name of the payee, although it is also possible for the drawer to write cash instead of the payee’s name. A ‘cash’ cheque is presented to the bank by the designated person who is responsible for handling business cash. It is also used to withdraw cash that the business will use to pay for transactions that are settled in cash. For some banks, it is also possible for a business owner to issue a cheque with no name of payee, apart from the cash cheque. This type of cheque is called a bearer cheque. This means that the bank will pay the amount stated to any person (bearer) who presents the cheque to the bank. An example of a bearer cheque is as presented in figure 1.1.

pg013_narration3: Figure 1.1: Bearer cheque This cheque does not mention the payee. This means that the amount written on the cheque is payable to any person who presents it to the drawer's bank. This implies that when such cheque is lost or stolen, the money can be paid to an unintended person. Bearer cheques are therefore rarely used in practice, because
pg014_narration1: of the security risk involved. The drawer has an option to issue an open cheque or a crossed cheque. An open cheque instructs the drawer’s bank (drawee) to pay the amount stated to the payee. The payment can either be made in cash or by depositing the amount in the payee’s bank account. Figure 1.2 illustrates an open cheque.

pg014_narration3: Figure 1.2: Open cheque The cheque is open because it does not have a crossing. This implies that the amount in the cheque can be paid to the payee in cash. The payee, however, still has an option to deposit the cheque in his/ her account. On the other hand, a crossed cheque instructs the bank to deposit the amount stated on the cheque to the payee’s account, without the option for the drawee to pay the amount in cash to the payee. Crossing is normally done by drawing or indicating two vertical lines on the face of the cheque. Some banks may add the words ‘A/C payee only’ which insist that the amount has to be deposited to the payee's account. For security purposes, most banks would by default have the cheques crossed, but give the drawer an option to ‘open’ the cheque by signing on the vertical lines crossing the cheque. pg015_narration2: Figure 1.4: Crossed Cheque with the words ‘A/C payee only’ Transacting using cheques is safe and convenient because the trader does not carry a lot of cash when making payments or collecting money from customers. The trader will be issuing cheques to suppliers and collecting cheques from customers. Banks normally keep records of transactions on each of the customers’ bank accounts. On the other hand, the customers will also have to make their own records of transactions with banks. Transactions made by the trader through cheques, and other transactions between the trader and the bank are recorded in a bank account. Recording transactions in the bank account To a business, a bank account is a type of cash book in which transactions with a bank are recorded. It therefore applies the same rules of debit and credit that apply in recording transactions in the cash account. These are: (a) Debit the bank account for transactions that increase the bank balance, for example, deposits of cheques. (b) Credit the bank account for transactions that decrease the bank balance, for example issue of cheques. When a cheque is received by the business, there may be an option to present it for payment (cash collection) from the drawer’s bank or deposit the cheque in the business’ (payee’s) account, depending on the type of cheque. For the purpose of this book, the cheques received by the business, whether open or crossed, are deposited into the trader’s bank account. To record a depositing of a cheque to the businesses` bank account, one will therefore debit the bank account and credit the drawer`s account in the ledger. It should also be remembered that when the business operates more than one account (either with the same bank or with different banks), separate bank accounts will have to be maintained in the ledger for each such account.

Balancing the bank account Balancing a bank account follows the same procedure that business follows when balancing the cash account or any other ledger account. Like the cash account or any other asset account, the normal balance for a bank account is Example 1.2 a debit balance. A debit balance in the bank account means that the business has money in the bank. However, it is possible for a business to have a credit balance in the bank account in some situations. This happens when the business has withdrawn more money than the amount available in the account. The credit balance on the bank account is known as an overdraft. Many banks allow customers to have an overdraft, as one of the forms of loan once a customer has fulfilled some conditions. Example 1.2 shows how transactions are recorded in a bank account where an account has a debit balance. Two-column cash book A cash book with two amount columns is called a two-column (double column) cash book. It is called two-column cash book because it has two amount columns on each side, one column records cash transactions, and the other column records bank transactions. The bank column records transactions made through cheques, cash deposits and other transfers of funds into the bank. On the other hand, the cash column records receipts and payments made using physical cash, cash deposits and cash withdrawals from bank. Usefulness of a two-column cash book The two-column cash book is useful because: (a) It makes it easier to monitor cash transactions because all the cash flow is viewed on the same place. (b) The business manager can see the cash and bank balances at any point in time and make appropriate decision. This can be possible with the use of technology, for example, computer systems in preparing a two-column cash book. Preparation of a two-column cash book This cash book operates in the same way that the cash account and the bank account would separately operate. The only difference is that two separate amount columns are used, on the debit side and on the credit side. The cash column is used for cash transactions and the bank column is used for recording bank transactions. The other columns remain the same as in separate cash/ bank accounts or any other ledger account. Posting transactions to the two-column cash book Recording transactions in the two-column cash book uses the double entry principle. This means all transactions representing increase of cash and bank balance are
pg019_narration1: recorded on the debit side of the cash and the bank columns, respectively. Similarly, all transactions leading to decrease of the cash balance and bank balances are recorded Example 1.4 on the credit side of the cash and bank columns respectively. pg022_narration1: Contra entries in the two-column cash book Example 1.4 indicates that the posting of entries in the two-column cash book is done in the same way as the separate accounts for cash and bank. However, it is possible to have transaction that affects both the cash account and the bank account. In this case, the transaction involves a transfer of cash into bank or cashing funds from the bank. A double entry made in such a case is called a ‘contra’ entry. ‘Contra’ is a Latin word for ‘opposite’. A contra entry can therefore be defined as an entry made on both sides of a two-column cash book on separate columns. It may either include a debit in the cash column and a credit in the bank column (drawing of cash from bank for Example 1.5 business use) or a debit in the bank column and a credit in the cash column (depositing business cash into bank). It is called contra entry because the two entries are made on the opposite sides of the cash book. For contra entries, there is no need for more posting to complete the double entry. This means that the entry in the cash column has its corresponding entry on the bank column on the opposite sides of the two-column cash book. The vice versa is also true. An example 1.5 includes contra entries in the transactions. The example also shows how to complete the double entry for each transaction. Three-column cash book A three-column cash book is a cash book that is prepared with three amount columns on both sides (debit and the credit). It has one additional column from the two-column cash book. The third column is designed to record cash discount. The three-column cash book is, therefore, a cash book with three amount columns, namely: the cash column, bank column and discount column. When a business has more than one bank account, each account will have a separate column, but the cash book will still be known as the three-column cash book.
pg030_narration1: Discounts, cash discount and credit terms The term discount refers to a reduction in price that one enjoys while dealing with a business especially in purchasing a product. There are various reasons for which businesses give discounts to customers. These reasons give rise to the three types of discounts, namely quantity, trade and cash discount as follows: (a) Encouraging purchase on large quantities – in this case, a business may have a policy of giving some price cut (mostly expressed in percentage) to all customers purchasing goods exceeding a certain quantity or a certain value. Such a price cut is called a quantity discount. (b) Psychological attraction of customers, traders may give price reduction to customers. This may be communicated using price tags that show original price and reduced price (sometimes indicating percentage of price reduction) and thus, attracting customers to the shop. This kind of discount is called a trade discount. (c) Encouraging credit customers to pay promptly most traders will give credit terms to customers. Credit terms specify the latest date on which the customer must pay the amount due to the trader. However, to encourage early payment, it is common for businesses to offer cash discount. This is the discount that is recorded in the three-column cash book. The quantity and trade discounts are not recorded in the books of accounts. This is because for those two discounts, the actual price (net of the discount) is the one that is shown in the invoice, which is a source document to record the transactions in the books. Credit payment terms and cash discount When goods are sold on credit, the seller has to specify credit terms to the customer. The credit terms specify the date to which the amount on the invoice must be paid. They may also include a cash discount as an incentive to pay before the due date. A cash discount is a reduction from the invoice price when a customer pays within a specified period. There are two main types of credit terms: credit terms without cash discount and credit terms with cash discount. Credit terms without cash discount
pg030_narration2: These are credit terms that do not include cash discount. In other words, there is no difference between the customer who pays within a day and the one who pays at the end of the credit period, as long as payment is made within the specified period. The terms can either be stated in a sentence, such as ‘payment within 30 days’ or use abbreviations such as f/30, meaning the full amount is payable within 30 days. Credit terms with cash discount These are credit terms which state the latest date at which the payment should be made. However, they also specify a discount (usually in percentage) to be
pg031_narration1: enjoyed if the payment is done within a certain period, as early as possible. An example of such terms could be expressed as, ‘5% discount if payment is made within 10 days, full amount payable within 60 days’. This can also be expressed in abbreviated form as "5%/10, f/60". For example, if the business sold goods for TZS 100,000 and offered a "5%/10, Preparation of a three-column cash book f/60" terms on the invoice, the customer will pay full TZS 100,000 if payment is done any time after the 10 days discount period. However, if the customer pays within 10 days of the discount period, the amount paid is only TZS 95,000. This is because 5% of the TZS 100,000 amount invoiced i.e. TZS 5,000 is deducted from the invoice amount. The three-column cash book has an addition of discount column, which is absent in a two-column cash book. A petty cash book is a separate cash book specifically maintained to record small cash payments, also known as petty payments. This book is usually operated by a specific cashier known as petty cashier. The petty cash book records petty payments such as office expenses, postage, telephone, stationeries, cleaning expenses, sundry expenses using columns that are designed to each category of expenses that the business may pay for using the petty cash fund. Petty cash cannot be used to purchase non-current assets, because they usually require large amount. When preparing the petty cash system, the business would normally have a policy that states which types of payments are settled with petty cash fund. The policy should state the limit of the amount of any single payment to be made through petty cash as well as the petty cash period. The petty cash period is the period between receiving the petty cash float and petty cash replenishment. The imprest system
pg037_narration2: The petty cash system works where the main cashier delegates petty cash payments to the petty cashier. The petty cashier is therefore provided with an agreed amount of cash known as petty cash float for the purpose of making petty cash payments. The cashier continues to use the petty cash for making various payments and records the transactions until the end of the period, or until the amount is finished. At the end of this, the petty cashier submits the details of payments and relevant source documents to the main cashier. The main cashier then makes a replenishment of the amount spent so that a new petty cash period can begin. The replenishment of the petty cash float is known as reimbursement. This kind of operation is known as an imprest system, and the petty cash float is also referred to as imprest amount.
pg038_narration1: The name imprest is historically associated with a Latin word ‘imprestare’, meaning ‘to lend’. Imprest sytem works not only for processing petty cash transactions, but also other business for larger transactions. The imprest system for petty cash is the system in which the petty cashier periodically receives a specified amount of cash from chief cashier. The petty cashier will be required to maintain all the documents (vouchers and receipts) that evidence payment from such amount and the amount to be restored by the chief cashier. In other words, the chief cashier ‘lends’ the petty cashier a specific amount of cash for use in various cash transactions. It remains as an imprest (loan) until evidence in terms of documents (petty cash vouchers and receipts) is submitted to the chief cashier to justify the payments. Ideally, the petty cashier will have to refund the money to the chief cashier when he or she fails to provide evidence (source documents) for the expenditure. Traditionally, many businesses use the petty cash voucher (abbreviated as PCV) as a source document for payments from the petty cash, although the PCV can be complemented with receipts or other documents from third parties. Usefulness of petty cash book and the imprest system The use of petty cash book and the imprest system is important for the following reasons: (a) It assists in the regulation of petty expenses. This is because each petty payment will be associated with a petty cash voucher that is backed up with evidence for the payment. (b) It enables easy detection of errors. If there is an error in petty payments, it is detected within the petty cash system. This would have been difficult to detect when all payments are handled through the main cash book. (c) It reduces burden to the chief cashier, who would have been responsible to record every tiny payment. (d) It helps in detection of fraud (improper use of cash). This is because the chief cashier can verify the petty cash book with the petty cash vouchers and other relevant supporting documents. (e) It saves time in posting transactions. This is because the petty expenses are batched up and posted periodically, for example, weekly to the respective ledger accounts.
pg038_narration2: (f) It helps in training junior accounting staff to handle cash responsibilities. Preparation of the petty cash book For a proper record of different expenses in the petty cash book, it is important to organise the book logically. The best way to organise it is to make a column for each major category of repetitive transactions of the petty cash. There may therefore be a column for transport, stationeries, refreshments. Total Cleaning Motor expenses Stationeries Travelling Other expenses Note: PCV – Petty cash voucher The petty cash book has separate column assigned to each specific category of expenses. These columns are called analytical expense columns. It also has a column for other expenses, which is used to record expenses that do not fall within any of the analytical columns. When entering a transaction in an analytical expense column, the petty cashier also records the same in the total column. The identity of the source document, the petty cash voucher (PCV) number, is recorded in the specific column.
pg040_narration1: The receipt column records the receipt of cash, normally petty cash reimbursement. This is done either at the end of each petty cash period, or after spending the whole amount of the petty cash imprest. Recording transactions and balancing the petty cash book This involves recording the following: (a) Receipt of the petty cash float from the main cashier This is recorded on the receipts column of the petty cash book, and its corresponding entry is made on the payments side of the main cash book. (b) Making different payments from the petty cash Each payment is recorded on the appropriate analytical expense column. A record is also made on the total column on the payments side of the petty cash book. (c) Receipt of reimbursement from the main cashier This is recorded on the receipt side of the petty cash book, and its corresponding entry is made on the credit side of the main cash book. Reimbursement can be made at the end of the imprest period or at the beginning of the next imprest period. (d) Balancing of the petty cash book The petty cash book is balanced in the same manner as any other cash book. An important thing to note is that the petty cashier should balance the receipts column against the total column of the payment side. If the reimbursement is done at the end of the imprest period, the balance of the petty cash book will be equal to the imprest amount. This is because recording the reimbursement will restore the balance to the imprest amount. pg054_narration1: Correction of Book-keeping errors and the Trial balance Introduction Books of accounts may contain errors. Book-keeping errors may originate from the source documents, from entries in the books of prime entry, ledger posting, or at any other stage in the accounting cycle. In this chapter, you will learn errors and the correction of errors in the trial balance. The competencies developed will enable you to make journal entries and relevant ledger postings to correct errors and prepare an adjusted trial balance. Think Making errors when preparing the trial balance Errors in the trial balance Every transaction made by the business is supposed to be entered and posted using the double entry system. The amount entered for each transaction must match with a respective source document. Further, each ledger account is supposed to be appropriately balanced, and the general ledger balances are normally summarised in the trial balance from time to time. A trial balance requires that debit and credit balances must be equal. However, some errors may occur due to mistakes made by book-keepers in recording, posting, or totalling. This may lead to discrepancies between debits and credits. Therefore, all errors must be identified and corrected. Meaning of book-keeping errors Book-keep ing errors are mistakes committed at any stage in the book- keeping process. They can be made by omitting an entry, entering a wrong amount in the books of original entry, entering a transaction in the wrong book of original entry, inappropriate posting to the ledger,
pg055_narration1: wrong computation of ledger balances, or even wrong preparation of the trial balance. The effect of book-keeping errors is that the affected account balances will not reflect the transactions that have taken place in the business during the period. At the end of the financial year, adjustments are made to the balances for some items, after which, the balances are used in the preparation of financial statements. When book-keeping errors occur at any stage, the resulting financial statements will be misleading, if such errors are not corrected. The causes of book-keeping errors can be summarised as follows: (i) Failure to record the correct amount from source documents. (ii) Omitting some items from the source documents when entering transactions in the books of prime entry. (iii) Making entries to a wrong account. (iv) Failure to make appropriate application of the double entry principle. (v) Making arithmetical mistakes when summing up amounts in special journals/ daybooks or when calculating balances for different ledger accounts. Sources of book-keeping errors in the trial balance These refer to the causes of errors that occurs in the process of preparing a trial balance. These causes often arise due to human mistakes, system problems and procedural weakness. The following are examples of sources of errors occurring in the trial balance: Lack of accounting knowledge: the book- keeper may lack or may have insufficient accounting knowledge and skills leading to recording incorrect figure. Clerical mistakes: these may occur due to incorrect totalling or transferring balances during recording of transactions. Carelessness: this occurs when book- keeper enter wrong figures, skipping transactions and reverse entries when preparing the trial balance. Technical errors: these arise due to problems in accounting software or system failures leading to miscalculations. Fraud or intentional errors: these occurs when a person deliberately manipulates records when extracting the trial balance to hide financial information. Types of book-keeping errors There are two broad categories of errors which are grouped depending on how they affect the trial balance agreement. These categories are: (i) Errors that do not affect the trial balance agreement.
pg055_narration2: (ii) Errors that affect the trial balance agreement. For the purpose of making appropriate correction of errors, it may be useful to understand the type of error in each categories.
pg056_narration1: Book-keeping errors that do not affect the trial balance agreement A trial balance agrees when the total of debit balances equals the total of credit balances. The trial balance will agree even if some types of book-keeping errors exist in the books of accounts, provided that the total value of debit entries made is equal to the total value of credit entries made. This also happens whenever the total of credit balances listed in the trial balance is equal to the total of debit balances, irrespective of the correctness of such balances. Therefore, trial balance will agree even if there is existence of one or more errors because: (i) There is an error that affects both a debit balance and a credit balance by the same amount, or (ii) There is an error in which an entry has not been recored in the books of accounts for that particular transaction, or (iii) There are two independent errors that cancel each other (with equal amount on debit and credit side). Considering these situations, there are six types of book-keeping errors that do not affect the trial balance agreement. These are: 1. Error of omission This is an error which occurs when the transaction is not recorded in the books of accounts. For example, a purchase of goods for cash TZS 345,000 is not recorded in the books of accounts. This transaction should have been recorded by making a debit entry of TZS 345,000 in the purchases account and a credit entry of TZS 345,000 in the cash account. When this is not done, the trial balance will agree because the entries are omitted from both the purchases account (debit side) and the cash account (credit side). This kind of error can be detected by tracing source documents (in this case the cash payment vouchers) to the journal and the ledger.
pg056_narration2: 2. Error of commission This is an error in which an entry is made to a wrong personal account that tends to be in the same class of account as the correct account, in which it should have been made. An example of this error happens in either the sales ledger or purchases ledger, in which a transaction is entered in a wrong personal account of a debtor or creditor, especially when the names of such persons have some similarities. For example, a TZS 250,000 sales of goods to Hawa Mwalimu has been debited in the account of Hawa Maalim, who also happens to be in the sales ledger of the business. This transaction was supposed to be debited in Hawa Mwalimu’s account, but was posted to Hawa Maalim. The posting to the general ledger, in this case, the trade receivables account and the sales account will not be affected by this error. The trial balance will therefore, agree even if this error has been made in the subsidiary ledger accounts of Hawa Mwalimu and Hawa Maalim. This error can be discovered by vouching subsidiary ledger entries to special journal entries and to the source documents and confirm whether the names in the source documents match with those in the books.
pg057_narration1: 3. Error of principle This kind of error happens when an entry is made to a wrong class of account. This error does not affect trial balance agreement, because a debit entry and a credit entry are made; but one of the entries is made to a wrong class of account. An example of an error of principle is a situation where a shop owner has bought shelves for use in the business and debited the transaction in the purchases account instead of shop furniture account. Doing this will overstate the figure of purchases and understate the figure of non-current assets (furniture) of the business. Although not affecting the trial balance agreement, an error of principle would lead to misleading figures in the financial statements. To discover an error of principle, one can review transactions from source documents to journal and ledger entries. 4. Error of original entry This error occurs when the original journal entry and ledger posting are completed in the appropriate accounts, but the amount recorded is wrong. For example, a cash payment of TZS 100,000 for wages is entered in the journal as TZS 1,000,000 which is then posted to the ledger. This means that the transaction was recorded in the wages account and cash account as TZS 1,000,000 instead of TZS 100,000. The error of original entry would in many cases be a result of additional (or omitted) zero in the figure. It could also occur as a result of transposing two digits in the figure, for example, TZS 980,000 is recorded as TZS 890,000. The trial balance would still agree in this case, since the problem starts with the original (journal) entry. This means that the same incorrect amount will be used for all accounts affected by the transaction.
pg057_narration2: 5. Error of complete reversal of entries This error occurs when entries are posted in wrong sides of accounts concerned. Reversal of entries occurs when a debit entry is made in the account that should be credited and a credit entry is made in the account should be debited. If this is done, the trial balance will still agree, because total debit entries and balances will be the same as the total credit entries and balances. An example of this is where a receipt of cash TZS 204,000 from a debtor is debited to the trade receivables account (which should have been credited) and credited to cash account (which should have been debited). This can be discovered by tracing the source documents to the journal entries. 6. Compensating errors These are two or more errors whose effects on the credit and debit balances happen to cancel each other. This is a situation when there are errors in the balances of two accounts with the same balances in nature, for example, an undercast of a debit balance and an overcast of another debit balance. An example is where there is an error in balancing accounts, where a rent expense account balance is TZS 45,000 more than it should have been, while at the same time wages expense account has a balance undercasted by TZS 45,000. The trial balance would still agree since the errors cancel each other. Another situation is where there are two accounts with opposite balance in nature.
pg058_narration1: There is an undercast of a debit balance and an undercast of a credit balance by the same amount, respectively. For example, the balance of sales account was undercasted by TZS 50,000; the salaries account was undercasted by TZS 50,000. These errors will not affect trial balance because they will cancel each other. In this case, the errors involve the same amounts and thus cancel each other. Such errors are discovered by tracing and vouching, together with recasting the ledger accounts. Considering the given examples, it can be noted that compensating errors are not a common thing in accounts. This is because it is rare to have such errors involving equal amounts and affecting opposite sides. However, there is one common situation where compensating errors can be found. This happens when there is an error in calculating the totals on a special journal. To understand this, you may need to refresh your understanding of the postings from the special journals. (a) Individual entries made in the special journals (daybooks) are posted to the sales ledger and purchases ledger (individual accounts of debtors and creditors) as follows: (i) For the sales journal, posting is done to the sales ledger by posting to the debit side of the individual debtors accounts. (ii) For the sales return journal, posting is done to the sales ledger by posting to the credit side of the individual debtors accounts. Book-keeping errors that affect trial balance agreement The double entry principle requires every debit entry to have a corresponding credit entry. A corresponding entry is an entry involving the same amount made on the opposite side of the other account relating to the transaction. There are errors that when made, the trial balance extracted at a particular date would not agree. Whenever the total amount in debit entries made is not the same as the total amounts of credit entries
pg060_narration1: made, the trial balance will not agree. Any book-keeping error that affects the trial balance agreement is a unilateral error. A unilateral error affects one part of the double entry required for a transaction, or one account in the ledger. While it is difficult to imagine all the possible errors that would cause a trial balance not to agree, it is possible to have some general categories of such errors. These categories are: 1. Single entry made for a transaction (omission in one account) In this error, either a debit entry is made without a corresponding credit entry, or a credit entry is made without a corresponding debit entry. This situation leads to trial balance disagreement when is done. This is because balancing of a trial balance depends on the application of double entry system. An example of this is where receipt of cash TZS 34,000 from Twilumba, a credit customer, has been recorded only in the trade receivables account. This transaction should have been debited in the cash account and credited in the trade receivables account. Recording it only in the trade receivables account leaves an error on the cash account. This causes the trial balance disagreement. 2. Use of different amounts to make ‘double entry’ In this error, both a debit entry and a credit entry for a transaction are made. However, the amount debited is different from the amount credited (in many cases one of them is correct, but it may also happen that they are both incorrect). In any case, as long as the amount debited is different from the amount credited, the trial balance will not agree. As a matter of fact, the entry made is not even supposed to be called a double entry, because the transactions are not recorded in equal amounts. An example of this would be where a credit sale of TZS 58,000 is recorded in the sales account as TZS 58,000, while in the trade receivables account it is recorded as TZS 58,800. In this case the trial balance will not agree.
pg060_narration2: 3. Completing ‘double entry’ in the same side of both ledgers concerned This happens when a transaction is recorded in two accounts concerned, but either debited in both accounts or credited in both accounts. This kind of recording is not double entry because corresponding entries must be made on opposite sides of accounts. When this happens, the trial balance will not agree because there will either be too much of the credit balances, or of the debit balances. For example, a receipt of interest from bank may be debited in both the cash book and the interest income account. 4. Errors in balancing ledger accounts or extracting balances to the trial balance Balancing errors may happen when balancing ledger accounts. These are also called casting errors. In book-keeping, the word ‘casting’ means adding a column of figures. So, the addition error in which the total shown is higher than the correct sum is called overcasting error. The opposite is an undercasting error. When there is a casting error in balancing accounts, the trial balance will disagree, unless there is
pg061_narration1: two casting errors that cancel each other. An example of such errors is where the total value of trade payables on the credit side is TZS 860,000, and the total value on the debit side is TZS 675,000,the balance in this account is supposed to be TZS 185,000 but recorded as TZS 165,000. It is also possible to have correct balances in the ledger, and a mistake arises in picking the balances during manual extracting to the trial balance. An incorrect amount can be picked, for example picking a total instead of a balance, or transposing digits in the balance. When this happens, the trial balance would disagree. For example, is where a TZS 650,000 balance on equipment account is shown in the trial balance as TZS 560,000. 5. Errors related to misplacing ledger balances in the trial balance This error may happen when extracting the trial balance. A debit balance extracted from the ledger is taken to the credit column of the trial balance, or the vice versa. An example is where a correct balance of sales account is placed in the debit column of the trial balance. The trial balance will not agree unless there is a coincidence that another balance of the same amount is also erroneously placed on the credit column. General approach to undertaking correction of book-keeping errors Deliberate efforts should be made to identify book-keeping errors in the accounting records. Once identified, the errors should be corrected. The general approach to correcting errors requires the following to be done in respect of each error: (i) Identify the correct entries that should have been made for the transaction; (ii) Find out the entries that were made; (iii) Make journal entries to make necessary correction(s). The correct entry to be made will involve a double entry whose effect is to both offset the erroneous entry made and make the correct entry. After the correction, the books should show a position as if the correct entry had been made in the first place. For the purpose of this book, the focus will be on correcting general ledger balances, except for situations where an error affects only the subsidiary ledger, for example, when correcting an error of commission. Correction of book-keeping errors that affect trial balance agreement These errors are unilateral; meaning that the error is made in one of the accounts involved in recording the transaction. In case, it is a casting error in balancing an account, the entry to correct will be crediting (provided that the casting error increased debit balance or reduced a credit balance). The vice versa is also true. The entry required to correct an error which affects trial balance does not necessarily require double entry as was the case with errors that do not affect trial balance agreement. Instead, the corresponding entries for these errors are made in a temporary account opened for special purpose. This account is called a suspense account. Suspense Account A suspense account is an account that is used to temporarily record a balance that cannot be explained at a particular moment. Traditionally, a suspense account is used by businesses as part of general ledger to record unclear entries that require clarification. A good example is when a business notices a credit entry has been made in its bank statement, meaning that someone has made a deposit in its account. While waiting for clarification of who made the deposit and for what
pg070_narration1: Activity 2.3 purpose, this amount will be placed in a suspense account. Once the clarification is obtained, the amount will be posted to the appropriate general ledger account. When the trial balance totals fail to agree, a balance is inserted temporarily in the side with a lower amount of total. Doing so will make the total debit balance and total credit balance to be the same. For example, when the total credit balances is TZS 10,200,000 and the total debit balances is TZS 9,750,000, a debit balance of TZS 450,000 is inserted to make both totals TZS 10,200,000. The account name given to this balance is suspense account. When errors that affect the trial balance are corrected, double entry is completed in the suspense account. When all errors have been corrected, the balance in the suspense account will be zero. For this reason, a suspense account balance will no longer appear in the trial balance. It may also happen that not all errors that affect the trial balance agreement have been discovered and corrected at the time when financial statements are being prepared. In this case, the suspense account would still have a balance. When the suspense account exists up to the date of preparing the financial statements, the balance would be reflected in the statement of financial position. The balance will be shown as a current asset or current liability, depending on whether it is a debit balance or a credit balance. Another is a situation where the suspense account will be eliminated after posting the correcting entries.

Adjusting the trial balance An adjusted trial balance is a trial balance that contains updated balances after correcting all the errors. This is prepared after all the entries made to correct errors have been posted to the ledgers and new balances obtained. In case there were some errors affecting the trial balance agreement, the suspense account would be opened and entries posted to it. In real life, there would be several revisions of the trial balance after the original trial balance has been prepared. pg090_narration1: Chapter summary 1. Book-keeping errors may occur by omission of entry, entering a wrong amount in the books of original entry, entering a transaction in the wrong book of original entry, wrong computation of ledger balances, or even wrong preparation of the trial balance. 2. The processes for discovering and identifying errors involve making sure that source documents exist for each transaction and are systematically arranged and filed to simplify tracing each transaction from the source document to the relevant journal. 3. There are two broad categories of errors, namely; errors that do not affect the trial balance agreement and errors that affect the trial balance agreement. 4. The errors that do not affect the trial balance agreement include error of omission, error of commission, error of principle, error of original entry, error of complete reversal of entries and compensating errors. 5. Identifying and correcting errors is crucial for maintaining accurate financial statements and ensuring the reliability of accounting records. 6. A suspense account is used by a business as a part of the general ledger to record unclear entries that require clarification. pg097_narration1: Chapter Three Reconciling bank account with cash book balances Introduction Businesses that conduct transactions through the banking systems need to have a system to constantly check the records of their bank transactions. This is facilitated by periodically comparing the bank column of their cash book against the statement received from the bank with details of transactions on their bank account. For any differences in entries and balances, an appropriate explanation will have to be sought and clarified. In this chapter, you will learn the bank reconciliation statement and adjusted cash book. The competencies developed will enable you to describe bank reconciliation statement, compare bank statement and cash book, make appropriate adjustments in the cash book, and prepare a bank reconciliation statement. Think Operating a business without reconciliation of cash book and bank statement balance Bank reconciliation statement A bank reconciliation statement is a statement prepared for the purpose of reconciling the bank balance as per cash book and the bank balance as per bank statement. A typical bank reconciliation statement begins with the cash book balance, adds and subtracts the relevant reconciling items and ends with the bank statement balance. The statement can also start with the bank statement balance and finish with the cash book balance. The actual structure of a bank reconciliation statement is illustrated in the next sections.
pg098_narration1: Importance of bank reconciliation statement The importance of preparing bank reconciliation statement can be summarised in the following points: (i) It helps in identifying possible errors in transactions. These include errors in the cash book and in the bank statement. (ii) It helps for the business to have an updated cash book and determine the bank balance to be reported in the financial statements. (iii) It is useful in tracking receipts such as direct credits, and expenses such as bank charges, penalties and update the ledger accordingly. (iv) It may assist in discovering ‘difficulty’ customers. Such customers might have a tendency to delay payment through technicalities, such as issuing post-dated or erroneous cheques. It is possible to discover this when a business experiences and investigates a tendency of dishonoured cheques from one customer. (v) It helps to detect fraud, for example stolen cheques cashed without the knowledge of the account holder, or altered cheques. To get maximum benefits of this, the bank reconciliation process should be done by a different person other than the cashier who is responsible for handling cheques. (vi) Bank reconciliation is also a required standard control procedure or activity for cash management. Bank statement This is a statement that shows transactions between the bank and its customer for a particular period as recorded by the bank. It is traditionally issued monthly by the bank, but may be issued at different intervals or at a specific date on customer’s request. The bank statement has columns for date, details, debit, credit and balance. The debit column of the bank statement reflects withdrawals, and credit column reflects deposits; it is opposite to the cash book. The balance column shows a balance of the customer’s account after every transaction. In other words, the balance is updated in real time after every transaction.

Steps in performing bank reconciliation The bank reconciliation process involves the following steps: (a) Balancing the cash book at the specified date. This can be done at the end of the month or any other date where reconciliation is required. (b) Obtaining a bank statement to the date of reconciliation. The bank statement should cover the same period as the cash book prepared in step (a). (c) Comparing entries in the cash book prepared in step (a) with the entries in the bank statement obtained in step (b) to identify the adjusting and reconciling items. (d) Adjusting the cash book using the cash book balance and the adjusting items obtained in step (c). (e) Preparing the bank reconciliation statement. Identification of adjusting and reconciling items This is done by making a comparison between the cash book and the bank statement. The comparison is made on each individual entry in the cash book and in the bank statement. Since the rules for recording transactions in the cash book and the bank statement are the opposite of each other, comparison is made between entries on the opposite sides of the records. This means a comparison is made between entries on the debit side of the cash book and the credit column of the bank statement. Comparison is also made between entries on the credit side of the cash book and the debit column of the bank statement. With exception of errors in either of the two records, the following would be the results of the comparison: (a) Items on the debit side of the cash book not matched with items on the credit column of the bank statement. These would represent uncredited cheques and cheques that the business had received and deposited during the period but dishonoured by the drawers’ bank(s), or they have not yet cleared due to some reasons.
pg100_narration2: (b) Items on the credit side of the cash book not matched with items on the debit column of the bank statement. These would represent unpresented cheques. These may also include cheques that the business has issued ,but the bank has dishonoured for some reasons, not yet deposited by the payee or not yet cleared due to some reasons. (c) Items on the credit column of the bank statement not matching with
pg101_narration1: items on the debit side of the cash book. These would represent direct deposits and transfers made to the business bank account. They could also include interest income from the bank. (d) Items on the debit column of the bank statement not matching with items on the credit side of the cash book. These would represent direct debit for standing orders and bank charges made to the business bank account. (e) Items that are matched in terms of description but have different figures in the two records. These suggest existence of errors either in the cash book or in the bank statement. Reasons for inconsistencies of cash book and bank statement Cash book (bank column) and bank statement are supposed to give identical balances at a given date because they both record the same transactions. However, in reality the two are unlikely to have same balance due to some reasons. The following are the reasons for the inconsistencies between cash book and bank statement balance. Unpresented or outstanding cheques An unpresented cheque is a cheque which the payee has not yet presented to the bank for payment. Cheques issued by the business during the month and not yet presented for payment within the month
pg105_narration1: will cause a difference between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance at the end of the month. This is because such a cheque will only appear in the cash book, but would not appear in the bank statement. Uncredited cheques An uncredited cheque is a cheque which the business has received and deposited into the bank, but the bank has not yet completed clearing the cheque with the drawer’s bank. The amount must have been debited in the cash book when the cheque was lodged to the bank, but will not appear on the credit column of the bank statement until when the respective cheque is cleared. Uncredited cheques are also called uncleared cheques, uncleared deposits or deposits in transit. Dishonoured cheques A dishonoured cheque is a cheque that the bank refuses to pay (to honour) for various reasons. Cheques are dishonored for the following reasons: (a) The drawer has insufficient funds with the bank, for example, the drawer has a bank balance of TZS 1,240,000 and has issued a cheque for TZS 1,500,000. (b) The cheque has an error(s) on it, for example amount in words differs from the amount in figures. (c) It is not signed by the drawer, or the signature does not match the signature in the bank records. (d) If the payee has not signed the back of the cheque (endorsed) before presenting it to the bank. For some customers, the bank may want the payee or the drawer to stamp on the back of the cheque. (e) It is post-dated. A post-dated cheque is presented for payment before the issue date (date written on the cheque). An example of a post-dated cheque is a cheque that the date of drawing or issue is written as 1 st June 2023 but presented for payment on 31 st May 2023. (f) It is stale. A stale cheque is a cheque that is presented for payment at a date later than six months from the issue date or from the date it was drawn. An example of a stale cheque is a cheque drawn on 20 th September 2023 but presented to the bank for payment on 1 st April 2024.
pg105_narration2: Any dishonoured cheque would have already been recorded in the cash book, but not in the bank statement. It will therefore cause a difference between a cash book balance and the bank statement balance, until the business becomes aware that the cheque is dishonoured and reflect them in the cash book. When you are doing business and operate a current account, dishonoured cheques may happen in two sides, namely: (i) Cheques that the business has received and deposited to the bank but dishonoured by the drawer’s bank(s); and (ii) Cheques that the business has issued to different payees and dishonoured by its bank.
pg106_narration1: It is very important to recognise the difference between the two in terms of identifying them from the records, and making appropriate treatment for each when performing bank reconciliation. Bank charges These charges would not be recorded in the cash book until the business receives the bank statement, in which case a debit entry for the charges will be observed. Standing orders Payments through standing orders will appear only in the bank statements at the time they are made by the bank. They would not be reflected in the cash book until the business confirms their execution through receiving the bank statement or any other way of notification that the business considers formal and acceptable for recording transactions in its books. Direct deposits and transfers (direct credit) These will result in a difference between the balances when such deposits or transfers are made, and the business has not received a bank statement and updated the cash book. Errors Errors could occur either in posting transactions to the cash book or bank statement. These would lead to difference between the two records, unless there is a coincidence that the same error is made in both the bank statement and the cash book. Many key terms are directly linked to specific inconsistencies between cash book and bank statement. These key terms describe concepts used in reconciling bank account and cash book balances. Adjusted cash book and bank reconciliation statement When managing financial records, it is crucial to ensure that the cash book and bank statement reflect accurate and consistent balances. However, due to timing differences, errors, and unrecorded transactions, discrepancies often arise between the two records. Once a comparison has been made, an adjustment of the cash book can be done. An adjusted cash book is a cash book that is prepared to ensure the real bank balance is reported. The real bank balance reflects the transactions that the bank has completed on behalf of the account holder such as bank charges. In cases where errors exist in the cash book, the adjustment of the cash book will also include correction of such errors. Adjustment in the cash book will give the adjusted cash book balance. The adjusted cash book balance is up to date and is reported as a bank balance in financial statements. The main items involved in adjusting the cash book are those that the bank has recorded as direct debits and credits. On the other hand, the figures for standing order and bank charges have been reflected by crediting the cash book. This is the case for all adjusting items that were debited in the bank statement. In the absence of any errors in the cash book, the adjudted cash book results in the bank balance to be reported in the financial statement. Preparation of bank reconciliation statement using adjusted cash book balance When the adjusted cash book has been prepared, reconciling items are only considered when preparing the bank reconciliation statement. These include unpresented and uncredited cheques recorded in the cash book, but not in the bank statement. This is due to time lapse and bank process. Remember two balances are being reconciled here, that is the adjusted cash book and the bank statement balances. The bank reconciliation statement shows how the difference between these two balances is explained using the reconciling items. The bank reconciliation statement can be prepared starting with the adjusted cash book balance and ending with the bank statement balance. It can also be prepared by starting with the bank statement balance and ending with the adjusted cash book balance. Whichever balance is chosen to start with, it should appropriately reflect the effects of the reconciling items to arrive at the other balance.
pg109_narration2: Starting with adjusted cash book balance The treatment of reconciling items is derived from the effect that each reconciling item has on the relationship between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance. This means that when preparing a bank reconciliation statement, the unpresented cheques will need to be added to the adjusted cash book balance. On the other hand, the uncredited cheques cause the cash book balance to be higher than the bank statement balance. This is because the amount has already been debited in the cash book while the same amount has not yet been credited by the bank. For this reason, preparing a bank reconciliation statement starting with adjusted cash book balance involves deducting uncredited cheques from such cash book balance. Bank reconciliation statement with more items Bank reconciliation statement includes other items, such as errors and dishonoured cheques, when reconciling bank records of a business. Therefore, there is a need to know how to treat such items when adjusting the cash book and preparing a bank reconciliation statement. In the case of errors, the treatment depends on the kind of error and its effect on the relationship between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance. If the error is in the cash book, it is treated as an adjusting item. It is dealt with when preparing the adjusted cash book. It will be treated as a reconciling item if unadjusted cash book balance is used when preparing the bank reconciliation statement. On the other hand, if the error is in the bank statement, the usual procedure is to notify the bank so that they can make an entry to reverse the error. Such reversing entry is reflected in the next bank statement. This makes bank reconciliation an important process. While waiting for the rectified bank statement, the amount of the error will be treated as a reconciling item. As for a dishonoured cheque, it is important to consider two possible sides. One is where the cheque dishonoured is a cheque that the business has received and deposited with its banks. Another side is the case where the cheque is the one that the business has issued to its creditor and for one reason or another it is dishonoured by the bank. Cheques received or issued when dishonoured are further clarified in the following subsections.
pg115_narration2: Cheque received but dishonoured This is the case where the business has received a cheque from a customer and deposited it with its bank. Apart from noticing that it has not been credited in the bank statement when comparing the bank statement and the cash book, the business would also receive a notification from the bank that the cheque is dishonoured. The cheque will also be returned to the business, which can make further reference from the customer. In any case, the dishonored cheque will be treated as an adjusting item. This is because the cheque will have to be cancelled by the customer, who will issue a fresh cheque to the business for the intended payment. The cash book adjustment necessary for this dishonoured cheque is a credit entry. This is because the amount must have been debited in the cash book when this cheque was originally deposited into the bank. Cheque issued but dishonoured When the business issued the cheque, it must have credited the cash book. The problem could have started when the payee presented the cheque for payment.
pg116_narration1: When a cheque is dishonoured, it would not be debited in the bank statement. After dealing with the problem that led to the dishonour, the business will have to cancel the cheque and issue a fresh one. The entry for cancelling the cheque is to debit the cash book when adjusting it. Reconciliation in overdraft situation There are situations where at the end of the month the business will have an overdrawn balance with the bank. It may happen that both the cash book and the bank statement show an overdraft at the particular date. It may also happen that either the cash book or the bank statement shows an overdraft, while the other shows a favourable balance. Whatever the situation, the bank reconciliation statement can be prepared to reconcile the two balances either by adjusting the cash book or without adjusting the cash book. The approach is the same as learnt for favourable balances, only that it is important to be sure the balances should be treated appropriately as overdrawn balances. This is because the reconciling and adjusting items will have a different effect on overdrafts (negative or unfavourable balance) as compared with the effect they have on favourable balances. Preparing a bank reconciliation statement in an overdraft situation As was the case with favourable balances, reconciliation can be done starting by either the cash book balance or the bank statement balance. It is important to note that either the adjusted cash book balance (overdraft) or the unadjusted one can be used. One peculiar issue is that it is an overdraft, or an unfavourable balance. Therefore, the effect of the reconciling items on the relationship between the overdraft as per cash book and the overdraft as per bank statement will not be the same as it would be in case of favourable balances. The effects can be summarised as follows: (i) Items that normally cause the cash book balance to be lower than the bank statement balance will cause the cash book to have a higher amount of overdraft than the bank statement. (ii) Items that cause the cash book balance to be higher than the bank statement balance will cause the cash book to have a lower amount of overdraft than the bank statement. This involves a different treatment of the reconciling items when preparing the bank reconciliation statement. It can be done either without reversing the reconciling items or by reversing the reconciling items.
pg123_narration1: Reconciliation without reversing the reconciling items The same structure of the bank reconciliation statement that starts with normal balances can be maintained while reconciling in an overdraft situation. The key point is to recognise the fact that an overdraft is, arithmetically, a negative balance. This means that the overdraft (as per bank statement or as per cash book) can be presented as a negative figure, and the bank reconciliation statement can proceed as usual. It is also possible either to start with the cash book balance or the bank statement balance. This is done when one wants to avoid using negative balances to represent overdraft in the bank reconciliation statement. To be able to do this, the relationship between the reconciling items and the balances is re-examined. The unpresented cheques make the cash book balance lower than the bank statement balance, and their effect on the overdraft will be the opposite. pg138_narration1: Budgeting and budgetary control Introduction Managing resources effectively is important for small businesses to keep the business running smoothly. A cash budget helps business owners plan for the money flowing in and out, ensuring they always have enough cash to pay for expenses, such as rent, salaries and supplies. The budget helps business owners to make better financial decisions, avoid cash shortages, and stabilise their businesses. In this chapter, you will learn budgeting, budgetary control, and preparation of a simple cash budget. The competencies developed will enable you to prepare a simple cash budget. Think Operating a small business without preparing a simple cash budget Concept of budgeting and budgetary control Budgeting and budgetary control are essential tools for managing finances in businesses. A budget is a financial plan that outlines expected revenue and costs. Budgetary control ensures that the actual spending of a business aligns with the budget. This helps businesses to allocate their financial resources, avoid overspending, and achieve financial stability. A good budget should be realistic, clear, flexible and goal-oriented to support effective decision-making. Different budgeting approaches, such as incremental and zero-based, allow businesses to plan based on their financial goals. Understanding the features of a good budget and budgeting approaches enables enterprises to manage cash flow efficiently, reduce financial risks, and grow sustainably. Meaning of budgeting and budgetary control Budgeting refers to the process of carefully planning how to generate and spend money. It involves planning on how the funds (revenues) are expected to be collected and how are to be spent for different purposes over a specific period. It helps individuals, businesses,
pg139_narration1: and governments to allocate resources effectively and guide financial decision- making. Budgetary control refers to setting financial targets, comparing actual performance with the budget, and taking corrective actions to ensure business goals are met. It ensures efficient resource utilisation and financial discipline. Importance of budget A budget is crucial in helping businesses and individuals to manage their finances efficiently by tracking revenues and expenses. The following are the importance of a budget: Cash flow planning: A cash budget helps individuals or businesses to predict cash flows (inflows and outflows) to ensure liquidity. Planning for money: A budget helps businesses and individuals to understand how much money they will receive from different sources and how much they will spend to operate a business in the future. This enables them to plan for future expenditure such as salaries, electricity bills, and rent. Therefore, without a budget, unexpected expenses can cause financial problems. Ensure efficiency in cash utilisation: A budget ensures that money is used for essential expenditure, in accordance with the plan. It helps business owners to focus on what is necessary, such as purchasing stock, paying employees, or investing in business growth. Without proper budgeting, money may be spent on unnecessary things, leading to shortages. Making good decisions: When a business knows how much money it expects to have in a certain period, it can make better choices about spending and saving. A budget helps to decide whether to expand the business, buy new assets, or reduce expenditures. This avoids overspending and ensures that money is available when needed. Controlling costs: A budget enables businesses and individuals to track spending and avoid unnecessary costs. Business owners can identify areas of overspending and take steps to control it. This practice helps to save money and enhances financial stability. Monitoring performance: Businesses can compare their actual revenue and expenditure with the budget to check if they are on the right track. When actual spending exceeds the planned amount, they can identify ways to cut costs and stay within budget. This helps businesses to make improvements and work towards their financial goals.
pg139_narration2: Avoiding money shortages: A budget helps businesses to ensure they have enough money to pay for various business expenses, such as transport charges, salaries and wages and supplies. Without a budget, businesses and individuals can have difficulties of paying their bills, leading to financial problems.

Approaches to preparing a budget There are various approaches of preparing a budget, depending on the specific needs of a business. Each approach has its advantages and challenges. Some of the common budgeting approaches include: (i) Incremental budgeting:This method uses the previous budget as a starting point and adjusts based on expected changes. For example, if a business spent TZS 1,000,000 on rent last year and the rent increases by 5%, the new budget will include the updated rent cost of TZS 1,050,000. This approach is simple and easy to use because it does not require complex calculations. However, it may use previous spending patterns without checking if they are still necessary. Furthermore, it does not encourage cost-cutting or finding new ways to save money, which can lead to inefficiencies over time. (ii) Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB): This approach starts from zero. Every expense must be justified before it is included in the budget. Previous costs are not automatically carried forward; each department or expense must prove its necessity. This method helps to reduce wasteful spending because businesses carefully examine all expenses before approving them. However, it requires more time and effort to prepare since managers must justify every cost, making it a more detailed and demanding process. Despite this challenge, ZBB ensures that resources are allocated efficiently and only necessary expenses are included.
pg140_narration2: (iii)Activity-based-budgeting :This budgeting method focuses on the activities that generate value for the business rather than just previous expenses. The budget is developed by identifying key activities and estimating how much they cost. For example, if a business plans to increase customer engagement, it may allocate more money to marketing and customer service activities. A business may decide to spend TZS 3,000,000 on advertising if it expects this will increase sales. This approach helps businesses to spend money more effectively.
pg141_narration1: However, a good understanding of cost drivers and business processes is required. Otherwise it will be difficult to implement. (iv) Value-based budgeting. This approach allocates money based on the business’s priorities and long-term financial goals. Businesses do not just continue with the past spending patterns, but determine which areas are most important and allocate resources accordingly. For example, if a company values innovation, it may set aside TZS 5,000,000 for research and development rather than administrative costs. This approach ensures that spending aligns with the business’s mission and vision, leading to long-term financial stability. However, it requires careful planning and a clear understanding of business priorities to ensure that funds are distributed effectively. Each budgeting approach serves a specific purpose, and businesses must select the one that aligns with their needs. By choosing the most suitable approach, a business can enhance financial planning, minimise unnecessary expenses, and ensure efficient resource use. Features of a good budget A well-prepared budget should have the following characteristics to assist individuals and businesses in managing their finances effectively: Realistic: A good budget should be based on accurate estimates of revenues and expenses to avoid financial problems. For example, if a shop owner expects to make TZS 500,000 in monthly sales, they should not budget for expenses of TZS 700,000 because it will lead to a cash shortage. Overestimating cash inflows or underestimating costs can lead to difficulty paying rent, restocking goods, or covering business expenses. Clear and simple: A budget should be clear and simple; so, everyone involved can easily understand and use it. It should be well-organised, listing revenues and expenditures in a straightforward format to avoid confusion. A simple budget helps individuals or businesses to track finances effectively and make informed decisions. For example, a small shop owner should clearly outline daily sales, rent, and stock purchases. If a budget is too complex, people may find it challenging to use or understand, resulting in poor financial management and unexpected losses.
pg141_narration2: Flexible: A good budget should allow for adjustments when financial situations change. For example, a farmer planned a budget assuming normal rainfall but later faced drought. In that case, he/she should be able to adjust costs, reducing non- essential expenses or finding alternative income sources. Flexibility ensures that unexpected events, such as emergency repairs or medical bills, do not disrupt financial stability. Comprehensive: A budget should include all sources of revenues and expected expenses to ensure adequate financial planning. For example, a food vendor should consider daily sales from food
pg142_narration1: and any additional revenue from catering services or the sales of soft drinks. Overlooking small costs, such as packaging or transport, can result in financial shortages, making it difficult to run the business efficiently. Time-bound: To facilitate a consistent financial review, a budget should be designed for a defined period, whether daily, weekly, monthly, or annually. For instance, a small business owner running a restaurant should create a monthly budget to cover all operating expenses, such as inventory, rent, and salaries, until the end of the month. Monitoring financial progress and making necessary adjustments becomes challenging without setting a clear time frame. Goal-oriented: A good budget should align with personal or business financial goals to ensure effective money management. For example, a young entrepreneur who expects to expand a poultry farm should budget for costs, such as buying more chicks, vaccines, and feeds while ensuring enough savings for future growth. A budget without clear financial goals may lead to unnecessary spending, delaying progress towards achieving essential objectives.
